scenes.text: Who owns AI art? AI models learned from millions of books, articles, songs, and pictures made by people. [1] So who owns what AI creates? And was it fair to train on all that work? [2] Let's untangle copyright and AI.

[1] Copyright is the legal right creators have over their original work. [2] It covers books, music, art, photos, and code. [3] Others usually need permission to copy it, [4] with some exceptions, like fair use, or fair dealing in India.

data.definition: The legal right creators have over their original work, controlling who can copy and use it.

scenes.text: There are three big questions. [1] Training. Is it legal to train AI on copyrighted work, without permission? [2] Outputs. What if the AI produces something very close to an existing work? [3] Ownership. Who owns what the AI creates, the user, the company, or no one?

On training, there are two sides. [1] AI companies argue that learning patterns from work is like a person reading books, and is transformative. [2] Creators argue their work was taken without permission or payment, and AI now competes with them. Courts in many countries are still deciding.

This is playing out right now. [1] Authors, artists, and news organisations have filed lawsuits against AI companies. [2] In India, the news agency ANI took OpenAI to the Delhi High Court. [3] Meanwhile, some AI companies now sign licensing deals, paying publishers for their content.

data.heading: Happening now
items: ANI vs OpenAI, Delhi High Court

scenes.text: [1] What about ownership of AI outputs? [2] If a human makes strong creative choices, and edits the work, copyright may protect the human parts. [3] If the AI makes it entirely, from one short prompt, many places, including the US Copyright Office, say it can't be copyrighted.

data.heading: Can you own it?
rows: Pure AI from a short prompt

scenes.text: Here's a common myth. [1] People think, if an AI made it, it's free to use in any way. [2] AI outputs can still copy protected characters, logos, or styles too closely. For commercial use, check the tool's terms, and be careful with famous brands, and characters.

data.myth: If AI made it, it's free to use any way.
data.fact: Outputs can still copy protected characters or logos. Check the tool's terms for commercial use.

scenes.text: Quick quiz! Can a picture made entirely by AI from a short prompt usually be copyrighted in the US? [1] Pause and think, and if you get it right, comment below! <pause 3.2> [2] Usually no, because copyright needs meaningful human authorship!

data.question: Pure AI image from a short prompt — copyrightable in the US?

scenes.text: Let's recap. [1] Copyright protects creators' original work. [2] The big questions are training, outputs, and ownership. [3] Lawsuits and licensing deals are shaping the rules right now.
